title: One family (Genesis Rabbah 24:7)
hook: Akiva names love your neighbor as the great principle; Ben Azzai names the book of Adam's generations, one human family
tomorrow: why would Noah plant trees he meant to cut down?

segments.voice: Yesterday: don't ruin my world, a garden handed over as a gift. Today, the people it was handed to.

Ask a group of friends for the one rule that sums it all up, and you'll get as many answers as friends. Two sages had that argument about the whole Torah. Rabbi Akiva named a line from Leviticus: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Ben Azzai named a different line, one that's easy to skim past, from a list of names in Genesis.
screen: `ONE RULE THAT SUMS IT UP?` → `AKIVA: LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOR.` → `BEN AZZAI: A LIST OF NAMES.`

segments.voice: His verse: "This is the book of the generations of Adam. In the day that God created man, in the likeness of God made He him." A family tree. Ben Azzai calls it a greater principle. Why pick a list of names over love? Because love your neighbor leaves a door open: who counts as my neighbor? The family tree shuts it. Every person you meet comes out of that one book, made in the likeness of God. Genesis Rabbah adds Rabbi Tanhuma's sharp line: don't say, since I was put down, let my fellow be put down too. If you do, know whom you're putting down: one made in God's likeness. So, who is my family? In Ben Azzai's answer, everyone in the book of Adam. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words. Christians read in the book of Acts that God "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth." The same picture: one family, from one start. And one honest difference. Ben Azzai argues from a Torah genealogy and God's likeness. In Acts, Paul says it in a speech in Athens that ends by pointing to Jesus, raised from the dead. Two traditions, each speaking from its own book, standing close on this one.
screen: `A FAMILY TREE OVER LOVE?` · `WHO COUNTS AS MY NEIGHBOR?` · `KNOW WHOM YOU'RE PUTTING DOWN.` · `ONE BLOOD, IN ACTS.` · then, large: `ONE FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring back one face from today that you don't know: a cashier, a driver, someone in line. Hold that face for a few breaths and say inside, from the book of Adam. Then let a second face come, and a third, and let the family grow until the bell.
One family: Ben Azzai's great principle, the book of the generations of Adam. Everyone in one family tree, each made in God's likeness.
Pocket this one: one family, the stranger in line included, all from the same book. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Ben Azzai's and Rabbi Akiva's sayings are often studied side by side in Jewish classes on how to treat others; the verse from Leviticus is also read in the synagogue in its yearly turn.

chat.meaning: Ben Azzai's one family and Acts' one blood stand close, each said from its own scripture. Close isn't the same as identical.

Ben Azzai.meaning: a sage who names Adam's family tree the great principle

Rabbi Akiva.meaning: a sage who names love your neighbor the great principle

Rabbi Tanhuma.meaning: a sage who warns against shaming one made in God's likeness

Acts.meaning: a book of the Christian New Testament

Leviticus.meaning: the third book of the Torah
